text_blocks.snippet: James Watson and Francis Crick discovered the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953, relying heavily on the crucial X-ray diffraction images captured by Rosalind Franklin and research from Maurice Wilkins.

James Watson and Francis Crick: American biologist Watson and English physicist Crick built the correct 3D physical model of the DNA double helix at the University of Cambridge. They published their findings in April 1953.

Rosalind Franklin: English chemist and X-ray crystallographer at King's College London whose famous "Photograph 51" and precise data provided the essential proof of the helical structure. Her data was shown to Watson without her knowledge or permission.

Maurice Wilkins: Colleague of Franklin who shared her X-ray images with Watson. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962. Franklin had died of cancer in 1958 and was excluded from the prize. Nature +4
If you'd like, I can share more about Photograph 51 or how Chargaff's rules helped them solve the puzzle.

perspectives.author: stem357
perspectives.title: Rosalind Franklin was a pioneering scientist whose work was crucial to the discovery of the DNA double helix. Using X-ray crystallography, she captured images of DNA's structure, including the famous "Photo 51," which provided key insights into the molecule's helical shape. However, without her knowledge or consent, her colleague Maurice Wilkins shared this data with James Watson and Francis Crick, who used it to build their model of DNA. While Watson and Crick were awarded the Nobel Prize for the discovery, Franklin’s contributions were largely overlooked during her lifetime. perspectives.author: interestingpedia
perspectives.title: Rosalind Franklin’s contribution to discovering the structure of DNA transformed modern biology, yet her role remained overshadowed for decades. Her X-ray diffraction image, famously known as *Photo 51*, provided crucial evidence for the DNA double helix. While James Watson and Francis Crick went on to publish the model and later receive the Nobel Prize, Franklin’s contribution received little recognition during her lifetime. She died in 1958 at the age of 37, and because Nobel Prizes are not awarded posthumously, she was never considered for the honour. Today, Rosalind Franklin is widely recognised as one of the most important scientists in the history of molecular biology—a reminder that groundbreaking discoveries are often built on the work of people history initially overlooks.

perspectives.author: themillionairewomensclub
perspectives.title: For six years, Rosalind Franklin carried a discovery that had the power to transform biology forever. In 1952, her remarkable work on Photo 51 provided one of the clearest views of DNA's helical structure and became a cornerstone of modern genetics. Despite the significance of her contribution, recognition did not come easily. Her marriage ended under public scrutiny, and she faced professional and personal challenges that would have discouraged many from continuing their scientific journey. Franklin remained committed to research and continued producing groundbreaking work in virology and molecular science. Her dedication to discovery never wavered, even when faced with criticism, injustice, and the lack of acknowledgment she deserved during her lifetime. She passed away from ovarian cancer at only thirty seven years old, but her legacy continues to inspire generations of scientists. questions_and_answers.answer: The famous Watson and Crick paper was not a stand alone paper. It was published beside the cryptographic evidence in a second paper. The problem was in 1953 no one thought they were right. The editor of Nature did but there was a lot of diversity of opinion. Linus Pauling thought it was a triple helix for example and his opinion carried a lot of weight. The Nature editor did not ask for it to be peer reviewed as he was happy with the two papers. If it had been the referees might have suggested not publishing it. Roll forward a few years and the double helix is now an accepted fact. Sadly Franklin had died in the interim from cervical cancer and was quietly overlooked. Sexism may well have played a role but being dead didnt help. The weird thing is DNA does not gave a single structure. Whle the bulk is a double helix parts are triple and even quadruple helices.

questions_and_answers.question: The DNA’s ‘double helix’ structure was discovered thanks in part to Rosalind Franklin. Today is her birthday! In 1962, James Watson, Francis Crick, and Maurice Wilkins confirmed the molecular structure of DNA by relying heavily on Franklin’s hypotheses and photographs of DNA strands created with X-ray diffraction. The three men won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the double helix structure of DNA. While Franklin did not win a share of the Nobel Prize despite her essential contributions, her work has not been forgotten.

questions_and_answers.answer: This is a pretty tricky question. I'm not 100% convinced the 1953 discovery of the structure of DNA changed ideas of heredity all that much. The beginning of the 20th century saw the 're-discovery' of Mendel's pea experiments which really boosted the field of genetics. So, by the 1950s scientists had a pretty good idea of how simple genetic inheritance worked, although the physical structure of the genetic material was still a mystery. There was also tension between ideas of evolution; extremely simplified this was Darwinists vs. Lamarckians. So basically they kind of had the idea that there was genetic "stuff" like chromosomes etc, but really until 1953 there was no molecular genetics in the same way there is today. If you are interested in the history of genetics, James Watsons book "The Double Helix" is a fascinating examination of science at the coal-face. It shows exactly how much the race towards this discovery was very much shooting in the dark. There are many great primary sour…

questions_and_answers.answer: Answer: James Watson and Francis Crick Explanation: The discovery of DNA's structure is one of the most significant breakthroughs in the history of science. James Watson and Francis Crick are credited with discovering the double helix structure of DNA in 1953 at Cambridge University. Their groundbreaking work laid the foundation for modern molecular biology and genetics. However, it's important to understand that Watson and Crick's discovery didn't happen in isolation. They built upon crucial research conducted by other scientists. Rosalind Franklin, a British chemist, played a vital role by using X-ray crystallography to capture detailed images of DNA. Her famous "Photo 51" provided critical evidence about DNA's helical structure and the spacing between its components. Maurice Wilkins, Franklin's colleague at King's College London, also contributed valuable X-ray diffraction data. questions_and_answers.answer: The woman you're thinking of is, notably, Rosalind Franklin. Her specialty was X-ray crystallography, and she worked with Maurice Wilkins and Raymond Gosling in the early 1950s, continuing their previous work, to apply X-ray diffraction to produce images of DNA. Watson and Crick's models were built and confirmed by data gathered by Franklin, Wilkins and Gosling; the images allowed them to discount previous models and identify the double helix. To say that Rosalind Franklin helped with the experiments is erroneous; she performed the experiments, along with her colleagues (and yes, other work on the problem of structure had been done by other groups around the same time). It would perhaps be more correct to say that Franklin performed the experiments and Watson and Crick interpreted them in more detail (as Franklin's group also came to the conclusion that a double helix was responsible for some of DNA's shape). questions_and_answers.answer: In the 1920's, Linus Pauling studied the brand new technique of X-ray crystallography which came into use for determining the arrangement of atoms in a crystal. In particular, Pauling deduced rules of interpreting X-ray diffraction images and used the technique to discover the helical substructure of several globular proteins, including hemoglobin. He proposed that DNA would have a triple helix structure. In 1949, Erwin Chargaff made very precise determinations of the percentages of each base (A, C, G, and T) in DNA isolated from cells of a variety of organisms. He demonstrated that two rules always held. The first was that the total amount of purine bases (A and G) equaled 50% as did the amount of pyrimidine bases (C and T). He also discovered that the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of G equals the amount of C.
